title: Iron-on pattern transfer
subtitle: Pressing a printed transfer paper onto fabric to stamp the design directly.
excerpt: Iron-on transfers are pre-printed on wax-coated paper. Pressing the paper ink-side-down onto fabric deposits the design permanently. The method is fast and works on any fabric that tolerates a medium iron. Most marks are permanent, so placement must be exact before pressing.
sourceNotes: Iron-on transfer embroidery designs developed in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Contemporary practice consistent with general needlework instruction.

glossaryTerms.definition: A sheet of heat-reactive paper with a design printed in wax-based ink on one side. When pressed with a hot iron, the ink transfers from the paper to the fabric surface, leaving a permanent guide line for embroidery.

content.text: is the fastest of all transfer methods for a single-use design. The marks are permanent on most fabrics, so there is no removal step. Position the transfer exactly before pressing; the marks cannot be moved once they touch a hot iron.
How to transfer an iron-on design
Press the fabric first to remove any creases.
Position the transfer paper ink-side-down on the fabric. The design will appear in reverse on the transfer sheet; the transferred result will be the correct way round on the fabric.
Pin or tape one edge to prevent sliding. Do not allow the transfer to shift once it touches the fabric.
Set the iron to medium heat (no steam). Press each section firmly for five to ten seconds. Lift and reposition; do not drag.
Lift one corner of the paper to check the transfer before removing the sheet fully.
Peel the transfer sheet away while still warm.

items.symptom: The transfer is patchy and some lines didn't transfer
items.cause: The iron temperature was too low or the pressure was uneven.
items.fix: Increase the heat slightly and press each section for longer. Work in small overlapping sections rather than trying to cover the whole design in one pass.

items.symptom: The transfer lines show outside the finished stitches
items.cause: The design was not covered completely by stitching.
items.fix: Iron-on transfer lines are permanent. Plan stitching to cover every line, or accept visible marks as part of the finished piece. For designs where marks must disappear, use a water-soluble or heat-erasable pen instead.

content.text: Iron-on transfers are best for kits and projects where the design is printed on the supplied sheet.
